entry: Geologic period, the third and shortest in the Paleozoic Era, spanning 23.5 million years from 443.1 Ma (million years ago) to 419.62 Ma. It lay between the [[Ordovician]] and [[Devonian]] periods, and began with the Ordovician–Silurian extinction events, when up to 60% of marine genera were wiped out. Vascular plants emerged during the Silurian-Devonian Terrestrial Revolution, and three groups of arthropods became fully terrestrial. Jawed fish diversified while jawless fish such as conodonts and ostracoderms declined. The system was named after the Silures, a Celtic tribe of [[Wales]].

Small, primitive, wingless insect, *Lepisma saccharinum*, of the order Zygentoma (formerly Thysanura). Its common name derives from its silvery light gray color and fish-like movement. It is nocturnal, eats carbohydrates such as sugar and starches, and can live in old books. Silverfish live up to three years and are cosmopolitan, found in Africa, the Americas, Australia, Eurasia and parts of the Pacific. They need moist places with relative humidity between 75% and 95%, and in cities they occur in attics, basements, bathtubs, kitchens and libraries. A female usually lays fewer than 100 eggs in her lifetime.

French mathematician and physicist. He worked on statistics, complex analysis, partial differential equations, the calculus of variations, electricity, magnetism, thermodynamics and elasticity. He predicted the Arago spot in an attempt to disprove the wave theory of [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]]. Although his interpretations of physical phenomena were often proven wrong, his contributions to mathematics have endured, and he showed that physical problems could suggest new mathematical ideas. He became full professor in 1806, succeeding [[Joseph Fourier|Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier]], and in 1827 succeeded [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] as geometer to the Bureau des Longitudes. He was said to be an extraordinarily successful teacher and published over 300 works, and his work in probability led to the [[Poisson distribution]].

Chinese historian of the [[Han dynasty|early Han dynasty]], regarded as the father of Chinese historiography. He wrote the *Shiji* (*Records of the Grand Historian*), a general history of China covering more than two thousand years, from the [[Yellow Emperor]] to the reign of [[Emperor Wu of Han]]. It became a model for official histories of later dynasties until the 20th century. Sima succeeded his father as court historian and helped create the Taichu calendar, promulgated in 104 BC. In 99 BC he spoke in defense of the general Li Ling, whom Emperor Wu blamed for surrendering after a campaign against the [[Xiongnu]]. Given the choice of execution or [[Castration|castration]], he chose castration in order to finish the work. He was also a gifted poet and prose writer.

Finnish military sniper, known as the White Death. He fought in the [[Winter War]] between Finland and the [[Soviet Union]] during [[World War II]], and is believed to have killed more than 500 enemy soldiers, the highest number of sniper kills in any major war. He is generally regarded as the deadliest sniper in history. In a private war memoir written in 1940, he estimated he shot around 500 Soviet soldiers; the memoir was hidden for decades and discovered in 2017. His reputation has also spread into metal lyrics and Japanese [[Manga|manga]].

English television personality, record executive and producer. He judged Pop Idol, The X Factor, Britain's Got Talent and [[American Idol]], and founded Syco Entertainment. Known for blunt, critical comments, he came to wide attention in 2001 on Pop Idol after a career as a record producer and talent agent in the [[Music industry|music industry]]. He helped launch the careers of Little Mix, Susan Boyle, Leona Lewis and [[One Direction]]. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2004 and 2010.

American musical duo of singer-songwriter Paul Simon and singer Art Garfunkel. One of the best-selling acts of the 1960s, they scored hits with "The Sound of Silence", a number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in a 1965 remix, and "Mrs. Robinson" and "Bridge over Troubled Water", both Record of the Year [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] winners. They split in 1970 but reunited several times, including a 1981 concert in [[Central Park]] that may have drawn more than 500,000 people. Their music featured in *The Graduate*. They sold more than 100 million records and were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1990.

American [[Gymnastics|artistic gymnast]]. With 11 Olympic medals and 30 World Championship medals, she is the most decorated gymnast in history. She is tied with Věra Čáslavská as the second-most decorated female Olympic gymnast, behind [[Larisa Latynina]]. Biles won the individual all-around at the 2016 and 2024 Olympic Games. She led the gold-medal-winning U.S. teams of 2016, the "Final Five", and of 2024, the "Golden Girls". At the 2020 Summer Olympics she withdrew from most events because of "the twisties", a temporary loss of proprioception while performing twisting elements. She has a record nine U.S. national all-around titles. In 2022, President [[Joe Biden]] awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

French [[Existentialism|existentialist]] philosopher, writer and [[Feminism|feminist]] activist. Although she did not consider herself a philosopher, she influenced feminist existentialism and feminist theory. Her best-known work, *The Second Sex* (1949), analyzes women's oppression and became a foundational text of contemporary feminism. She also wrote novels, such as *She Came to Stay* (1943) and *The Mandarins* (1954), and essays, biographies and memoirs, beginning with *Mémoires d'une jeune fille rangée* (1958). She met [[Jean-Paul Sartre]] while studying for the agrégation in philosophy. She won the 1954 Prix Goncourt and the 1975 Jerusalem Prize, and was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1961, 1969 and 1973.

Periodic motion in which a restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from an equilibrium position and acts toward it. The motion is a sinusoidal [[Oscillation|oscillation]] that continues indefinitely if no energy is lost to [[Friction]]; otherwise it becomes damped. Typical of a mass on a [[Spring (device)|spring]] obeying [[Hooke's law]], it has a single resonant frequency. The equation of motion is a [[Ordinary differential equation|second-order linear ordinary differential equation]] with constant coefficients, obtained from Newton's second law and Hooke's law. It also approximates a [[Pendulum|simple pendulum]] for small swings and models molecular vibration. Simple harmonic motion underlies the analysis of more complicated periodic motion through [[Fourier analysis]].

Transgression against divine law or, in some traditions, a universal moral code. The English word comes from Old English *synn*, rooted in a sense of being truly guilty. In [[Abrahamic religions|Abrahamic faiths]], sin is an offense against God: [[Christianity]] treats it as disobedience, redeemed through Christ's sacrifice, while Islam distinguishes minor and grave sins and Judaism describes it as missing the mark of God's law. In [[Hinduism]], *pāpa* (sin) is a demerit that ties a person to the cycle of rebirth. [[Buddhism]] has no concept of sin as defiance of a deity, holding instead that actions bring consequences through [[Karma|karma]], and it names five acts as especially heinous. In [[Shinto]], sin is impurity caused by external factors, and purification rituals restore harmony.

Peninsula of Egypt, the only part of the country located in West Asia. It lies between the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and the [[Red Sea]] and is a land bridge between Africa and [[Asia]]. Its land area is about 60,000 sq km (23,000 sq mi), with a population of approximately 600,000. Part of Egypt since the First Dynasty (c. 3100 BC), the peninsula was also occupied by the Ottoman Empire and the United Kingdom. Israel invaded during the [[Suez Crisis]] in 1956 and again at the start of the [[Six-Day War]] in 1967, and Egypt launched the [[Yom Kippur War]] in 1973. Israel withdrew in 1982 under the 1979 Egypt–Israel peace treaty, except for Taba, which was returned after arbitration in 1989. Today the peninsula is a tourist destination for its natural setting and rich [[Coral reef|coral reefs]].

Fractured Mexican drug trafficking organization and transnational crime syndicate based in Culiacán, Sinaloa. It began as a branch of the Guadalajara Cartel and became independent after the 1989 arrest of its co-founder, Miguel Félix Gallardo. Under Ismael Zambada García and Joaquín Guzmán Loera, it expanded into the global trade of [[Cocaine|cocaine]], [[Fentanyl|fentanyl]], [[Heroin|heroin]] and [[Methamphetamine|methamphetamine]]. Since 2024 an internal conflict has split it between followers of Guzmán's sons and of Zambada's son. The United States Intelligence Community considers it the largest and most powerful drug trafficking organization in the world.

Southeastern province of Pakistan, third-largest by land area and second-largest by population. Its capital, [[Karachi]], is the country's largest city and main financial hub. Sindh is bounded by the [[Arabian Sea]] to the south and borders Gujarat and Rajasthan in India to the east. Its landscape includes alluvial plains of the [[Indus River]], the Thar Desert and the Kirthar Mountains. Sindh is prominent for its Bronze Age history under the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]], and [[Mohenjo-daro]] is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Arabs conquered Sindh in 712 CE under the [[Umayyad Caliphate]], laying foundations for the Muslim period in South Asia. The [[Mughal Empire]] captured it in the late 16th century. The East India Company captured Sindh in 1846, and it became a separate province in 1936. It joined the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. Its culture is strongly influenced by [[Sufism]].

[[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan]] language and official language of Pakistan's [[Sindh]] province. It is written in a Perso-Arabic script in Pakistan and in Perso-Arabic and Devanagari scripts in India, where it is an official scheduled language. Sindhi is inflected, with five noun cases and two genders. Its name derives from *síndhu*, the Sanskrit name of the [[Indus River]], and it descends from [[Sanskrit]] through Middle Indo-Aryan. After the Umayyad conquest of 712 CE, Sindh was among the first Indian regions to encounter Persian and Arabic influence. Its literature includes the mystic poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, from the 18th century. More than 34 million people speak it in Pakistan and 2.7 million in India.

Fundamental trigonometric functions. In a right triangle, the sine of an acute [[Angle|angle]] is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, and the cosine is the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse. Their definitions extend to any real value through the [[Unit circle|unit circle]], and modern definitions use infinite series or differential equations. They also extend to complex numbers. They are commonly used to model periodic phenomena such as [[Sound|sound]] and [[Light|light]] waves, harmonic oscillators and day length.

Flag carrier of Singapore, with its hub at [[Changi Airport]]. It flies about 160 Airbus and Boeing passenger and freighter aircraft and was the launch customer for the [[Airbus A380]]. The airline has been a member of Star Alliance since April 2000. Its group includes Scoot, a low-cost carrier, and SIA Engineering Company, which handles maintenance across nine countries. Known for its "Singapore Girl" branding, Singapore Airlines has been ranked the world's best airline by Skytrax six times and is certified as a 5-star airline.

1952 American musical film by Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen. Starring [[Gene Kelly|Gene Kelly]], Donald O'Connor and [[Debbie Reynolds]], it depicts Hollywood's transition from [[Silent film|silent films]] to talkies in the late 1920s. Arthur Freed conceived it from songs written by himself and Nacio Herb Brown, and writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green set the story in the transition era. It was released nationwide on April 11, 1952, and was only a modest hit, but today is frequently cited as the greatest musical film and one of the greatest films ever made. It topped the AFI's Greatest Movie Musicals list, and Kelly's rendition of its title song ranked third among the greatest film songs. In 1989 it was among the first 25 films selected by the [[Library of Congress]] for the National Film Registry.

Music release with fewer tracks than an [[Album|album]], typically containing one song. Singles may stand alone or come before an album as lead singles. The format was defined in the mid-20th century by the 45, a 7-inch vinyl record with one song on each side. It was highly influential in [[Pop music|pop music]] and early [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]], and was used in jukeboxes. Digital singles became popular in the 2000s; the [[ITunes|iTunes Store]] accepts as singles releases of three tracks or fewer, each under ten minutes. Physical music is now mainly bought as albums rather than singles.

Indo-Aryan language of the Sinhalese people of [[Sri Lanka]]. Spoken by about 16 million Sinhalese people, it is also the first language of about 2 million other Sri Lankans as of 2001. It is one of the country's two national languages, along with Tamil, and is written in the Sinhalese script. The language shows [[Diglossia|diglossia]], with distinct written and spoken varieties. Early inscriptions from the 3rd century BCE are in a Prakrit similar to [[Magadha|Magadhi]]. Along with [[Pali]], Sinhala played a major role in the development of [[Theravada]] Buddhist literature. Its name comes from the Sanskrit for lion, sometimes glossed as 'abode of lions'.

Bowl-shaped plumbing fixture for washing hands, dishes and other purposes, also called a basin or washbin in the UK. Sinks have a tap that supplies hot and cold water and a drain that may include a strainer and an overflow-prevention device. Many, especially in [[Kitchen|kitchens]], are installed beside or inside a counter. In the late 18th century the washstand, a small table with a pitcher and bowl, served as a bathroom sink in the United States. From about 1820 to 1900 the dry sink evolved, with a wooden cabinet holding a trough lined with [[Zinc|zinc]] or lead. [[Stainless steel|Stainless steel]] is most common in kitchens and commercial applications, valued for cost, durability and ease of cleaning, though it is noisier than most materials. Other materials include soapstone, fire clay, [[Granite|granite]], [[Cast iron|cast iron]], [[Quartz|quartz]], [[Porcelain|porcelain]] and [[Copper|copper]].

Depression or hole in the ground caused by collapse of the surface layer. Most are caused by [[Karst|karst]] processes, the chemical dissolution of [[Carbonate|carbonate]] rocks such as [[Limestone|limestone]], or by collapse or suffosion processes. They are usually circular, from tens to hundreds of meters in diameter and depth, and may form gradually or suddenly. They are found worldwide. Human activity, such as the collapse of abandoned mines, causes collapses that are commonly and incorrectly labeled as sinkholes. In 2015 scientists reported active pits, possibly linked to sinkhole collapses, on the [[Comet|comet]] 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko.

Maritime disaster in the [[Atlantic Ocean|North Atlantic Ocean]] on April 15, 1912. The largest [[Ocean liner|ocean liner]] in service, RMS *Titanic* was four days into her maiden voyage from [[Southampton]] to [[New York City]] when she struck an iceberg on the night of April 14, with more than 2,200 people aboard. She sank about two hours and forty minutes later, with the deaths of around 1,500 people, one of the deadliest peacetime maritime disasters in history. Her wireless operators had received seven warnings of [[Sea ice|sea ice]]. She carried only twenty lifeboats, and many were launched before they were full. Almost all of those in the water died within minutes of [[Hypothermia|hypothermia]] and cold shock, while the RMS *Carpathia* rescued 710 survivors. Inquiries led to changes in maritime regulation, including the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) in 1914.

War of 1765–1769 between the [[Qing dynasty]] of China and the [[Konbaung dynasty]] of Burma, also called the Qing invasions of Burma. The [[Qianlong Emperor]] launched four invasions, considered one of his Ten Great Campaigns. Burmese forces defeated the first two, in 1765–1766 and 1766–1767. The third, led by elite Manchu bannermen in 1767–1768, penetrated within a few days' march of the capital, Ava, but the bannermen could not cope with unfamiliar tropical terrain and lethal endemic diseases. The fourth got bogged down, and field commanders agreed a truce in December 1769. The war claimed over 70,000 Qing soldiers and four commanders, and is sometimes described as the most disastrous frontier war the Qing dynasty ever waged. Burma's defense laid the foundation for the present-day boundary between the two countries.

Language family of more than 400 languages, native to Asia. It is second only to Indo-European in number of native speakers: about 1.4 billion people speak a Sino-Tibetan language, most of them among the 1.3 billion speakers of [[Chinese language|Chinese]] (Sinitic) languages. Other large members are Burmese (33 million) and the Tibetic languages (6 million). Most others are spoken in small, poorly documented communities in the [[Himalayas]], the Southeast Asian Massif and the eastern edge of the [[Tibetan Plateau]]. The family is traditionally divided into Sinitic and Tibeto-Burman branches, but its higher-level structure remains unclear because a common origin of the non-Sinitic languages has never been demonstrated. Early classifications included Kra–Dai and Hmong–Mien, a grouping still supported by Chinese linguists but rejected internationally since the 1940s.
